title: The professional's preparation: ideas cannot be turned on like a faucet
summary: Wilson argues a pro must back inspiration with learned knowledge and preparation so he can perform when not inspired.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, Milt, you're a professional too. In studio work, when that clock hits a certain time, you still have to play; you can't say that it's an off day or something. The pro plays when he has to play, and when he's finished, he's finished.
Rises to the occasion, right.
I noticed some of these athletic teams -- in certain situations, they just fall apart.
Uh huh.
And yet at other times, they can't lose. But the real pro never falls apart. He never falls, to me.
You got to go on, right.
If he really studies his work -- you see, and Milt probably has, too, I've got all sorts of bolsters, I know that in this type of work, you're working with

ideas, and no man can turn on ideas like a faucet, you know? Like all right, now the clock has hit three, we start. Ideas start flowing at three minutes of, and then bang, turn the faucet off and the ideas stop. You just can't do that.
Right.
So you have to bolster that flow of ideas with knowledge.
That's right.

One of the characteristics of the playing, when the ideas are flowing, you have to sit and learn the notes and memorize them, so you can play good when you don't have those ideas, or when you don't feel like playing -- you still can play good. Because you learn and study the characteristics of what you do when you're up and giving an inspired performance. You come as near it as you can by intelligence.
Oh, surely.

And that's the way the pro is. The guys who walk in, like these men who walk into the symphony hall at two o'clock in the afternoon, and the conductor raises his hand and they play the symphony. Everybody wasn't inspired, but they know enough to -- they can play, see, and they had good training so that when the time comes to perform, they do it.
And one of the secrets to that is to prepare
yourself -- if you prepare yourself, you be so nervous, your knees are knocking, and you can still play good.
But if you walk in there unprepared, your knees knock like they're gonna break in half.

And there's no excuse to stop, there's no excuse to stop -- when the music stops, if you are playing or recording a performance -- when the music stops, if you can't make that measure, you don't stop to fool around; you go into the next measure.
Absolutely, you have to.
You keep going.
Oh yeah, right.
You can't get behind.
